title: Swern activation
subtitle: DMSO and oxalyl chloride make the chlorodimethylsulfonium ion, losing CO₂, CO and chloride

reactants.caption: dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) + oxalyl chloride
hintTiers: DMSO's S–O bond is polarised: S⁺–O⁻. Which end is the nucleophile, and which atom of oxalyl chloride is the electrophile?
The DMSO oxygen makes a bond to a carbonyl carbon of oxalyl chloride, and that C=O π pair moves onto its oxygen. Two arrows.
DMSO oxygen lone pair → new O–C bond to a carbonyl carbon; that C=O π bond → lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Sulfur does have a lone pair, but it carries the positive charge here. The negatively charged oxygen of DMSO is the nucleophile.
Chlorine is not the electrophile; the carbonyl carbon it is attached to is.

misconceptions.arrowPattern: lp O3 -> σ O3-C6; σ C6-Cl5 -> lp Cl5
misconceptions.feedbackMessage: At a C=O carbon the nucleophile adds first and the π pair moves onto oxygen. Chloride leaves in the next step.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon. That carbon would have five bonds: move the C=O π pair onto oxygen.

tetrahedral.caption: tetrahedral intermediate
hintTiers: Which group on the tetrahedral carbon is the best leaving group?
The oxygen anion re-forms C=O and the C–Cl bond breaks, its pair going to chlorine. Two arrows.
Oxygen anion lone pair → C=O π bond; C–Cl bond → lone pair on chlorine.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Losing DMSO again just reverses the addition. Chloride is the better leaving group.
The C–C bond will break later. First the intermediate collapses and chloride leaves.

acyloxysulfonium.caption: acyloxysulfonium ion + chloride
hintTiers: Sulfur is positive and bonded to an oxygen that is part of a good leaving group. What does chloride do?
The chloride lone pair makes a bond to sulfur, and the S–O bond breaks with its pair going to oxygen. Two arrows.
Chloride lone pair → new Cl–S bond; S–O bond → lone pair on that oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Chloride adding to a carbonyl carbon would only swap one chloride for another. Sulfur is the electrophile that matters here.
SN2 on a methyl of the sulfonium ion is possible in principle, but attack at sulfur is much faster and leads on to the oxidant.

chlorosulfonium.caption: chlorodimethylsulfonium ion + chlorooxalate anion
hintTiers: The anion can break into three small, very stable molecules. Which ones?
Four arrows at once: the oxygen anion makes a C=O π bond (CO₂), the C–C bond breaks onto the other carbon, that carbon loses chloride, and its oxygen makes a third bond to it (carbon monoxide).
Oxygen anion lone pair → new C=O π bond; C–C bond → lone pair on the acyl chloride carbon; C–Cl bond → lone pair on chlorine; carbonyl oxygen lone pair → new C≡O π bond.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That reverses the last step. The anion falls apart into gases instead: this is what makes the activation irreversible.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right start: CO₂ is forming. The other carbon now has a lone pair and five electron pairs around it: let chloride go, and let its oxygen make a third bond to it.
Nearly there. The carbon of carbon monoxide has only six electrons: its oxygen gives a lone pair to make the C≡O triple bond.
Chloride does leave, but on its own it would leave a carbon with only six electrons. The C–C bond breaks at the same time and the CO₂ forms: draw the whole fragmentation.

steps.explanationAfterStep: The sulfoxide oxygen adds to a carbonyl carbon of oxalyl chloride, as any oxygen nucleophile adds to an acid chloride.
The C=O re-forms and chloride leaves. The DMSO oxygen is now part of a very good leaving group.
Chloride substitutes at sulfur: the chlorodimethylsulfonium ion, the real oxidant of the Swern.
The chlorooxalate anion falls apart into CO₂, CO and chloride. Two gases leave, so nothing goes back. (CO is toxic: Swern oxidations are run in a fume cupboard.)

mechanismSummary: The oxygen of DMSO adds to oxalyl chloride, and chloride is lost. Chloride then attacks the positive sulfur, pushing out a chlorooxalate anion, which falls apart into CO₂, CO and chloride. The product, chlorodimethylsulfonium chloride, is made at −78 °C and used at once to oxidise an alcohol.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 23
